title: HTTPS profile approval, revocation and `ward check`
description: Spec §9.1-9.2. Manifest is a request, not authority: developer approves an immutable normalized snapshot bound to project/root; any change to destination, method, auth, body or output policy, or unknown fields, invalidates it. `ward check` is local readiness only.

acceptanceCriteria.text: T13: changed URL, method, auth alias, body/output policy, binding, or unknown profile fields cannot reuse an approval
`ward check <profile> --json` reports missing binding/value/approval without any network I/O or value disclosure

plan: 1. Branch feat/WCLI-9-profile-approval off origin/dev; claim the task; record the design-settlement reading (bearer only in the first flow, non-bearer deferred) and file the deferred extension as WCLI-33.

2. Domain: a normalized approved-profile snapshot type with a discriminated auth union whose only implemented arm is bearer; normalization from the project manifest's profiles; unknown fields and unsupported auth types rejected rather than ignored.

3. Application: an approval port (developer gate, three-valued approved/declined/unavailable like the existing RegistrationApprover, never treating unavailable as consent) and a vault-backed snapshot store bound to the project and root.

4. Invalidation: at approval and at check, a declared profile must match the approved snapshot exactly on adapter, method, URL, auth scheme and alias, non-secret headers, body policy, output policy and binding; any change or unknown field refuses reuse (T13).

5. CLI: ward profile list/approve/revoke and ward check [profile] --json, local readiness only, no network I/O, no value or length or fingerprint disclosure; revocation invalidates future admissions only.
6. Tests: T13-class invalidation matrix over every snapshot field, ward check readiness and non-disclosure, unsupported-auth rejection, layer check, the full bun run check.
7. Independent review per spec 15 (opum-workflow reviewer), fix and re-verify findings, then deliver.

8. PR into dev carrying the closing evidence (PR number and CI run id, never a merge SHA), gate on every required context on the exact head SHA, squash merge, delete the local branch, and promote dev to main with git push origin origin/dev:main (main is one tracker-only commit behind and rides this promotion).

DESIGN-SETTLEMENT CHECK, RUN BEFORE STARTING (2026-09-29, at opum-agent's kickoff 03:40Z). The check was outstanding, not passed: WCLI-27's renewal note records that its session read ADR 0003 and spec 9.1-9.4 and stopped there.

QUESTION PUT: are the non-bearer auth schemes (custom API-key header, HTTP Basic) in WCLI-9 or deferred?

SOURCES READ FIRST-PARTY: WARD_MVP_AGENT_SPEC.md sections 5, 8, 9.1, 9.2, 9.3, 9.4, 14 and 15, and docs/adr/0003-profile-approval-authority.md read through lore. No tracker record and no doc decides the question; the spec is the only source.

READING: DEFERRED, and the spec settles it. Three clauses carry the reading. (1) 9.2 "Support Bearer authentication first", with 9.1's proposed manifest syntax declaring "auth": {"type": "bearer"}, makes bearer the first scheme and the only one the first flow names. (2) "Add a custom API-key header and HTTP Basic only if they pass the same safety tests" is conditional, and the condition is undischarged: the same safety tests are themselves being built here (T13-class approval binding, T14-class credential non-disclosure), so neither scheme can pass tests that do not exist yet. (3) "these are bounded extensions, not reasons to delay the first valid consumption flow" subordinates them to the flow, and spec 15's "Prove non-disclosure before widening the command surface" says the same. An extension is an addition to something that exists first, so it is not part of the thing it extends.

CONSEQUENCE: WCLI-9 and WCLI-10 deliver the first valid consumption flow with bearer as the only implemented scheme. The approved-snapshot schema models auth as a discriminated union so the extension is bounded, an addition rather than a migration, and an unsupported or unknown auth type is rejected at approval time under 9.2's unknown-field and no-runtime-override rules. The deferred work is filed as WCLI-33, depending on WCLI-10, with the "must pass the same safety tests" condition carried in its acceptance criteria.

ATTRIBUTION: the reading is this session's, made an execution choice by opum-agent's kickoff message conditional on the spec settling the question. It is recorded here rather than in an ADR because it decides a task boundary and not a system contract; opum-agent can correct it cheaply if it disagrees, and only WCLI-9's bearer path is built on it.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTE (2026-09-29). What landed and what a later reader cannot get from the diff.

BUILT. The manifest now carries profile declarations (src/domain/project-manifest.ts), a declaration normalizes to the approved snapshot (src/domain/profile.ts), approvals are stored in the vault bound to a binding (src/domain/vault-state.ts's profileApprovals collection), and the commands are ward profile list/approve/revoke plus ward check (src/application/profiles.ts, src/cli/main.ts, src/contract/manifest.ts). T13 is enforced where it is used: ward check compares the declared profile against the approved snapshot field by field and reports approval-stale with the differing field names, and a declaration the normalizer refuses reports as an invalid declaration rather than throwing, so one unreadable profile does not hide the others.

DECISIONS WORTH KNOWING, each with its reason. (1) An approval is bound to the BINDING, not merely to the project: spec 8 says ward profile approve "approves an immutable snapshot for this binding", so the record carries project, root, device and inode, and a second checkout of the same project has no approval. (2) The manifest carries profile declarations unvalidated and normalizeProfile judges them where they are used, deliberately unlike every other manifest field: validating them at parse would let a profile typo refuse ward secret, because readCheckout runs before every project command. (3) Approval and revocation both need an interactive terminal, on ADR 0003's sentence naming approve, grant and revoke as developer acts from a trusted terminal; a mid-question "unavailable" is never consent. (4) Prompts print values, results never do: the question carries the normalized operation to the terminal, and every result carries identifiers and state only, so no URL or header value can reach stdout. (5) ward check reports a missing binding instead of refusing, which is what AC1's "reports missing binding/value/approval" asks for; test reads the vault and the manifest and there is no transport port in this build, so it cannot reach the network. (6) Comparison is literal by design: header order and an omitted optional field are normalized (so they are not changes), while a URL differing only in a default port or a header name differing only in case is a different approved operation and needs approval again. (7) Bearer is the only scheme implemented; api-key and HTTP Basic are refused as unsupported, which is the WCLI-33 deferral made executable. (8) Restore now clears profile approvals along with bindings: clearing bindings alone would leave an approval unreachable today, but re-registering the same directory would make it live again, and T21 wants a restored vault's approvals inactive pending explicit review.

EVIDENCE. bun run check is green: typecheck, lint, format, layer check, and 494 tests across 19 files, of which test/profile.test.ts adds 63 cases. The T13 matrix is asserted through ward check rather than through the normalizer alone, one case per field the criterion names. The readiness case patches globalThis.fetch and asserts zero calls, with the declaration naming a real https destination so a request would be possible if any code made one.

TOOLCHAIN FINDING, carried here because it bit this task's own test file. In Bun 1.3.14, a top-level binding named declare in a .ts file is stripped as if it were a TypeScript ambient declaration: the definition and every bare-identifier call to it vanish, with no diagnostic and exit 0. Minimal reproduction: "function declare(value: string): void { console.log('ran', value); } declare('hello');" prints nothing under bun, prints normally as .js, and a differently-named function is unaffected; "const declare = () => {}" with "declare()" behaves the same way, while a member call such as holder.declare() is unaffected. This cost a debugging cycle here: a test helper named declare silently did nothing, and the tests that used it failed for a reason that pointed at the code under test rather than at the helper. Filed as WCLI-34 (a guard over this repository's own sources), and routed to opum-agent for fleet-wide propagation.

FINDINGS, most severe first, none fixed yet:

F1 (Medium) — the URL is validated as a PARSED url and stored as the RAW string, so an approved record does not pin one destination. src/domain/profile.ts:144-168: normalizedUrl judges new URL(value) (protocol, user-info, hostname) and returns value. Measured by the reviewer with three parsers: "https://api.example.invalid\@evil.example/steal" is judged host api.example.invalid by new URL while curl resolves evil.example; and "https:/api.example.invalid/x" (one slash) is accepted by Ward while Bun's fetch refuses it, so the approval can record an operation this build's own client cannot send. Only control bytes are refused today. Partly a DESIGN QUESTION the code itself names: does the approved snapshot pin the developer's text or the operation Ward would perform? Fix direction: store new URL(value).href (so the prompt shows what the validator judged), or refuse when the parsed href differs from the declaration. Exploitability today is nil (no transport in this build); it becomes WCLI-10's, whose parser decides. The reviewer ranks it first because the decision should be taken while the stored record's meaning is still free.

F2 (Low-to-Medium) — ward check and ward profile list print manifest-declared profile NAMES raw, including terminal control bytes. src/application/profiles.ts:389 and :427 interpolate entry.profile unescaped, while the prompt escapes every value (terminal-consent.ts:154-182) and parseProjectManifest bounds names by length only. Reproduced: a manifest key "evil\u001b]0;PWNED\u0007name" reaches output with ESC and BEL in both text renderers; the JSON path is safe and approve/revoke are safe because requireProfileName rejects the name first. Impact: control sequences from a tracked, agent-writable file into a terminal or a log. Fix: one escapeForDisplay call in each renderer.

F3 (Low-to-Medium) — the interactive approval gate has NO test, and the one named for it measures a different object. All 97 added lines of terminal-consent.ts (the prompts the developer actually reads) are executed only through FakeApprover, which returns a constant. test/profile.test.ts:1093 "the approval prompt, and only the prompt, shows the operation" records JSON.stringify(question) — the port payload, not the rendered prompt — so it passes if profileApprovalPrompt were deleted, printed the URL unescaped, or leaked the sentinel. The prompt parts are already injectable (isInteractive, writePrompt, readAnswer), so the fix is a few cases in test/terminal-consent.test.ts.

F4 (Low-to-Medium) — the "no network I/O" case cannot detect the failure it names. test/profile.test.ts:935-956 patches globalThis.fetch and counts calls, which misses node:http/https/net/tls, a fetch reference captured at module load, and a spawned curl. The property genuinely holds today — the reviewer grepped the tree and found no node:http/https/net/tls and no bare fetch( in src, test or scripts — but nothing enforces it, because check-layers.mjs restricts only relative imports, so node:https would pass the layer check. Keep the case (it carries a positive control) and add the structural half in the shape test/non-disclosure.test.ts:131 already uses, asserting no transport specifier is reachable from src/application/.

F5 (Low) — one check heading is FALSE about the state it reports. src/application/profiles.ts:376-378: when the checkout is unbound and the manifest declares no profiles, the heading says "Not ready: Ward would refuse to run at least one declared profile" while the next line says none are declared. Exit 6 is defensible; the sentence is the defect. Say the true thing, or let the binding reason carry it.

F6 (Low) — the new serializeProjectManifest profiles pass-through is unreachable today and untested. Its only caller (src/application/project.ts:231) is handed a manifest only for a fresh or restored one, so it never carries a non-empty profiles object, and no test covers it. Right behaviour to keep; nothing would notice if a later edit reverted it. Fix: one round-trip test.

F7 (Low, informational) — adapter and output can only ever be compared against themselves, because normalizeProfile refuses anything but "http" and "status" before a snapshot exists. So the "output policy changed" arm of T13 is exercised as an invalid declaration rather than a stale approval. Correct for a build with one output policy, and a coverage note rather than a hole: a regression that made output silently default would be caught by the refusal test, not by a staleness test.

F8 (Informational) — the tracker note this session wrote says test/profile.test.ts "adds 63 cases"; measured at eddace3 it runs 64. The note's other figure (494 tests across 19 files) checks out. The note is the artifact a later reader trusts, so the count is corrected here.

(1) DESIGN QUESTION, the reviewer's: the approval record carries no schema version of its own, so a future build that changed what normalizeProfile accepts would re-interpret old approvals through the new normalizer; the vault's formatVersion is the only version in the chain. Whether the approved-snapshot schema needs its own version is undecided. (2) For WCLI-10: build its header map with Object.fromEntries rather than obj[name] = value, because assigning a string to __proto__ is a silent no-op — the change's own use of Object.fromEntries round-trips a "__proto__" header exactly, measured. (2) THE TWO DESIGN QUESTIONS, SETTLED FROM THE SPEC AS EXECUTION, CITED HERE BEFORE WCLI-10 DEPENDS ON THEM.

(a) An approved snapshot pins the NORMALIZED OPERATION, not the developer's raw text. WARD_MVP_AGENT_SPEC.md read first-party this session: line 247, "The developer approves the normalized operation: adapter, exact method and URL, authentication scheme and aliases, permissible non-secret headers, request-body policy, output policy, and bound project/root"; line 259, "Only connect to the approved destination." Implemented: normalizedUrl returns the parser's canonical href, so one string is stored, displayed in the approval prompt, and later executed; and a declaration the parser would REWRITE is refused rather than silently resolved. The rewrite rule now covers both halves of the URL: the authority the developer wrote must equal the one the parser read (case-folded, a declared :443 the single fold allowed) -- which refuses user-info, the IPv4 number forms 0x7f000001 and 2130706433 that both read as 127.0.0.1, and a leading-zero port -- and the path, query and fragment must survive parsing byte for byte, which refuses encoded and literal dot segments and any character outside RFC 3986's unencoded set, a malformed percent escape, and a single-slash or backslash-bearing authority. Consequence for T13, recorded deliberately because it is the one place the settled reading changes what T13 means: comparison is over operations, so a respelling that names the same operation (host or scheme case, a default port, an added trailing slash, an empty query or fragment) is NOT staleness, while any change of destination is. The tests name both directions.

(b) The approved-snapshot collection carries its own version. Line 121: "Store versioned collections for projects, local bindings, secret records, sharing grants, approved profile snapshots, and a bounded audit history inside one encrypted snapshot." Implemented as a per-record snapshotVersion (currently 1, exported as profileSnapshotVersion): a record naming a version this build does not implement is refused as vault_format_unsupported rather than re-read through this build's normalizer. Per record rather than per collection, deliberately: records from different versions can sit side by side, and a collection-level version would have to claim a uniformity it could not guarantee. No migration is needed, and the reason is worth keeping: WCLI-9 is the first build to write an approval record at all, so no stored record predates the field and requiring it cannot strand a vault. The second review found the mechanism's weak point -- the constant was not bumped when the accepted set changed one commit after the field was introduced -- so the constant now carries the obligation in writing and a golden table of 22 accepted and refused spellings makes any change to that set fail a test.

finalSummary: WCLI-9 delivered the authority half of the first valid consumption flow: manifest profile declarations, the normalized snapshot a developer approves, approvals stored in the vault bound to project/root/device/inode, ward profile list/approve/revoke and ward check, with T13 enforced where it is used and no network I/O or value disclosure on any readiness path. Two design readings settled it and are cited on the record before WCLI-10 depends on them: an approval pins the normalized operation (spec 9.2/9.3), so the URL is stored as the parser's canonical form and any declaration the parser would rewrite is refused; and the approved snapshot carries its own schema version (spec 6.2), with a golden table of 22 spellings making the version-bump obligation mechanical. Two independent reviews ran: the first found eight issues, the second verified the fixes, found five more in the fixes themselves, and four of those are closed here (the authority rewrite rule, node:http2, the unescaped checkout root, the over-refused empty query), the fifth closed by the golden table. Verified by the full gate green locally on 502499a -- typecheck, lint, format, layer check 39 files 0 violations, 547 tests across 19 files -- by nine mutation proofs each reddening only the cases that name the behaviour, by the acceptance criteria's own command envelopes, and by the three required contexts on the head that merges.
